title: Misc. bug: Vulkan ARGSORT ne=[2048,1,1,1] only sorts half of the array on some devices
body:
### Name and Version

$ ./llama --version
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11188, commit e85e15cf6)
built with GNU 15.1.1 for Linux aarch64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Test code

### Command line

```shell
./test-backend-ops -o 'ARGSORT(type=f32,ne=[2048,1,1,1],order=0)'
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

- On Adreno A750
  - `maxComputeWorkGroupInvocations` is `2048`
  -  `maxComputeWorkGroupSize`: `[1024, 1024, 1024]`
- `use_small` is `true` in  `ggml_vk_argsort()`
- `pipeline_argsort_f32[10]` is used, which has `BLOCK_SIZE` of `1024`
- 2 workgroups are dispatched
- Only half of the array is sorted
- Test fails

I think the 2 workgroups end up sorting the first 1024 elements (so those end up being sorted twice while the other 1024 half remains unsorted).

title: eval bug: draft-mtp roughly halves prompt processing on multi-GPU layer split (single GPU is fine)
body:
### Name and Version

build 10499 (6d0549831), reproduces identically on 6c8dcaa7a (Aug 3)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

## Environment

- build 10499 (6d0549831), also reproduced on 6c8dcaa7a from Aug 3 — not recent
- Linux, CUDA 12.0 + Vulkan build
- RTX 4090 Laptop 16GB (internal) + RX 7900 XTX 24GB (RADV)


### Models

- models: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_XL / Q3_K_XL), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M —
  all with nextn_predict_layers=1
- -fa on, -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Just spent the last two days knees deep in benchmark after benchmark with a bench harness I built out as I tried to optimize my setup. Essentialy a llama-bench-replica for all the flags.

I found some anomolies with MTP. After doing my best to track them down, I'm convinced these are unnexpected behavior. tldr: MTP is still a net gain, but my pp drops from ~1k to ~500 t/s. Wins back on my workloads to pay itself off in the benefits on tg, but... I'm pretty confident that hit hints at a bigger issue. I do think tb4 is probably exacerbating the issue, but my suspicion is this is an issue for others with more standard setups as well.

To be clear, on single gpu, it's like a 3% penalty to use MTP. When I split across my two gpus, it's like a 100% penalty. something is off. and settings the `draft mtp device` flag to set it to one gpu gets me back only 8% of that loss.

## What happens

With `--spec-type draft-mtp` enabled, prompt processing drops to roughly half speed
whenever the model is split across two GPUs with `--split-mode layer`. On a single GPU
the overhead is small. Same model file, same flags, only the device assignment changes.

I went down a few wrong paths on this (thought it was my eGPU, then thought it was
CUDA-specific) so I ended up with a fairly complete matrix. 22k token cold prompt (huge code file + give me a code review of this),
prompt eval t/s from server timings:

| config | no MTP | draft-mtp | worse by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, RTX 4090 solo (CUDA) | 766 | 742 | 3% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, 7900 XTX solo (Vulkan) | 572 | 505 | 13% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M, 7900 XTX solo | 1593 | 1307 | 22% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 973 | 532 | 83% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 1007 | 555 | 82% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, Vulkan1+Vulkan2 layer split | 754 | 376 | 100% |

disclosure: *"no MTP" rows use --spec-type ngram-map-k4v, which doesn't touch prefill and matches
the no-spec prefill rate--I tested locally, match was within 1% when I did both on many runs.
And for clarity: last row is the same NVIDIA card via Vulkan instead of CUDA,
so no CUDA anywhere, and it's even worse. its no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the
same split. to be clear, llama-bench and llama-server rates agree within ~1% on the row where I have both. Row 6's no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the same split.

The `graphs reused` counter roughly halves with MTP on in every config (e.g. 960 ->
425 on the CUDA split pair, 897 -> 346 on Vulkan solo), but that on its own doesn't
seem to cost much... the solo rows eat the same reuse loss and barely slow down. The
expensive part only shows up when the layers are split across devices.

## Why I think this happens (or I should say, why AI tells me this is possibly happening--this is above my paygrade)

> In common/speculative.cpp the MTP process() hook runs a synchronous catch-up decode in
the draft context for every prefill ubatch (unless the model is mem-shared; the
"e.g Gemma4" comment). On a layer split that means every ubatch the pipeline between
the two GPUs gets broken by a decode on another context, so the ubatch overlap
(GGML_SCHED_MAX_COPIES) never gets going. That would explain why single GPU is nearly
free but any split pays ~2x regardless of backend.

You're the maintainers, you likely know better than me. I've been a dev since 2016, but I'm mostly a web dev, still learning the ropes on local AI

## Repro

```
# fast prefill:
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf -c 262144 -ngl 999 -fa on \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type ngram-map-k4v \
  --split-mode layer -dev CUDA0,Vulkan2 -ts 40,60 --jinja

# ~half speed prefill, only --spec-type changed:
llama-server ... --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 ...
```

Send any large cold prompt to both and compare `prompt eval time` in the timings.

## Related

Possibly connected to #26750 (draft-mtp acceptance collapse on CUDA vs Vulkan). I can
reproduce that one on this hardware btw (41% acceptance CUDA solo vs 64% Vulkan
solo, same Q3 file), though it's a different symptom (decode quality vs prefill speed).
Also #27306 crashes in the same draft-mtp prompt path on RADV. Seems possible someone else already found this exact code path, where it crashes for them?

Worth knowing, kind of mentioned above, I tried `--spec-draft-device CUDA0` on the split as a workaround. helps a little (532 -> 573, which I'm calling 8%), but doesn't recover the loss, so it doesn't look like it's about where
the draft context lives; the per-ubatch interruption of the target pipeline seems to
be the cost either way?

Thanks for everything you do, great fucking project.

## MTP gain?

I still run MTP despite this. On my setup it takes tg from ~17 to ~26-28 t/s (novel text; verbatim-heavy stuff spikes way higher). I logged ~4 days of real agent usage (139 requests) and my active time splits roughly 77% generation / 23% prompt processing — so eating the prefill hit and keeping MTP still nets me somewhere around 20-25% less total wall time than turning it off. MTP is still great even with a halving of pp speed, which is wild. But that the prefill cost looks like it's possibly all coming from a specific scheduling behavior. Would be huge to double the speed of 25% of my stuff, and probably would help many others.



### First Bad Commit

I don't know. What I can say is the bug was still present 250~ or so commits ago. I upgraded and rebuilt hoping that would fix it, no such luck. (6c8dcaa7a seemed to have the same issue. I just pulled main and rebuilt yesterday and that didn't fix it.)

```

llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf -c 262144 -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type ngram-map-k4v --split-mode layer -dev CUDA0,Vulkan2 -ts 40,60 --jinja
```

title: server : add Prometheus histogram for request context sizes
body:
## Motivation

When running llama-server with `--metrics`, the Prometheus endpoint exposes counters and gauges for throughput, token counts, and speculative decoding stats, but there is no visibility into the distribution of context sizes across requests. Knowing whether most requests are short (< 4k tokens) or long (> 64k) is useful for capacity planning, KV cache tuning, and monitoring workload characteristics over time.

## Proposal

Add a standard Prometheus histogram metric `llamacpp:request_context_tokens` that records the context size (prompt tokens) of each completed request. Key details:

- **Metric type**: Prometheus `histogram` (cumulative `_bucket`, `_sum`, `_count`)
- **Labels**: `model_name`, `model_alias` — allows per-model time series in multi-model / router setups
- **Default bucket boundaries**: `1024, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536, 131072, 262144`
- **Custom boundaries**: new `--metrics-ctx-buckets B1,B2,...` CLI flag (env: `LLAMA_ARG_METRICS_CTX_BUCKETS`)
- **Gated**: only emitted when `--metrics` is enabled (existing gate)

This follows the same patterns as the existing speculative decoding per-position counter.

## Example output

```
# HELP llamacpp:request_context_tokens Distribution of context sizes (in tokens) across completed requests
# TYPE llamacpp:request_context_tokens histogram
llamacpp:request_context_tokens_bucket{model_name="qwen3",model_alias="qwen3",le="1024"} 3
llamacpp:request_context_tokens_bucket{model_name="qwen3",model_alias="qwen3",le="4096"} 8
...
llamacpp:request_context_tokens_bucket{model_name="qwen3",model_alias="qwen3",le="+Inf"} 17
llamacpp:request_context_tokens_sum{model_name="qwen3",model_alias="qwen3"} 683947
llamacpp:request_context_tokens_count{model_name="qwen3",model_alias="qwen3"} 17
```

title: server: llama-server hangs before serving any request on Jetson Orin NX (aarch64, L4T 36.4.7) after the b8638->b9016 server rewrite
body:
## Environment

- Board: NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 16GB (sm87, unified memory, VMM: yes)
- L4T / JetPack 36.4.7, kernel 5.15.148-tegra, driver 540.4.0, CUDA 12.6
- llama.cpp tags `b9016` (846262d78) and `b11199` (86a24a182), both built via jetson-containers with `GGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_F16=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` for sm87
- Run inside `docker run --runtime=nvidia --network=host` (and same behavior outside docker)

## Repro

```
llama-server -m <any GGUF> --host 0.0.0.0 --port 11434 -ngl 99 -c 2048 --parallel 1 --jinja
```

Last output line:

```
0.37.437.187 I srv  llama_server: listening on http://0.0.0.0:11434
```

After that, never anything: `/health` and `/v1/chat/completions` hang (curl timeout), no request is ever logged, no error, no crash. The process sits in state S with ~0% CPU; `gdb -p <pid> -ex "thread apply all bt"` shows every thread parked in futex/lock waits.

## What we verified (all hang identically)

- Model-independent: tested Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.6-27B, and several
- `-ngl` 0..99, `-c` 1024..8192, `--parallel 1` and default 4
- `--no-warmup` on and off
- CPU-only (`-ngl 0`) and CUDA
- `--shm-size=8g` and default (64 MB)
- `GGML_CUDA_ENABLE_UNIFIED_MEMORY` set and unset
- `dmesg` clean - no driver/nvmap errors on any run

## Differential

- Older llama.cpp **b8638** (same board, same `docker run --runtime=nvidia --network=host`, same model file): serves fine. Its log shows the old server entry point:
  - `main: server is listening on http://0.0.0.0:11434`
  - `main: starting the main loop...`
  - `srv  update_slots: all slots are idle`
- New-style server (`srv llama_server: listening`, operator-based rewrite): binds the port, prints listening, then never enters the request loop.

Regression window: b8638 -> b9016 (378 commits; heavy server/kv-cache/checkpoint churn in that window, e.g. #22114 "refactor use checkpoint logic", #19493 "server: speculative checkpointing", #22155 "ggml-cuda: flush legacy pool on OOM").

## Ask

The post-b8638 server implementation hangs during startup (before serving any request) on Jetson/aarch64 with this driver generation. Is a tegra/aarch64 startup hang known in the server rewrite era? Happy to provide full gdb backtraces from the wedged process or test specific commits on this board within the b8638..b9016 window.

title: Misc. bug: YaRN configuration metadata is missing after converting PLaMo-3 models to GGUF
body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11200, commit 81bc6b83f)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Python/Bash scripts

### Command line

```shell
hf download pfnet/plamo-3-610m-fin-instruct --local-dir ./model
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype f16 --outfile ./f16.gguf ./model
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Recent PLaMo-3 models use YaRN, while some earlier PLaMo-3 models do not. The recent PLaMo-3 store their YaRN settings as flat config keys (rope_scaling_factor, initial_context_length) and build the dict at runtime in Plamo3Config.rope_parameters. The converter misses these settings and writes plain RoPE metadata to GGUF. As a result, the generated GGUF is missing the following parameters:

```
plamo3.rope.scaling.type
plamo3.rope.scaling.factor
plamo3.rope.scaling.original_context_length
```

title: [Bug] macOS Metal OOM & Compute error (-3) on Gemma 4 31B after update: Insufficient Memory with large default n_ctx

### Name and Version

version: 0.5.0 (build 11146, commit 7fe450e19)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000334 for Darwin arm64


### Operating systems

Mac

### GGML backends

Metal

### Hardware

Apple M5 Max, 128 GB Unified Memory

### Models

unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF (UD-Q8_K_XL)
mmproj: mmproj-F32.gguf

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Problem description
The model was working fine previously, but after updating llama.cpp to the latest master, llama-server fails to start inference and crashes with Metal Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. I am on an M5 Max with 128 GB of Unified Memory, which should be more than enough for a 31B model under normal context sizes.

The server loads the model successfully, but immediately fails during prompt processing, producing a "Compute error" and repeated "Insufficient Memory" errors on the macOS Metal backend.

### Environment
- OS: macOS Golden Gate 27.0
- Chip: Apple M5 Max
- Memory: 128 GB Unified Memory
- llama.cpp version: 0.5.0 (build 11146, commit 7fe450e19), built with AppleClang 21.0.0 for Darwin arm64

I ran the following command (without explicitly setting `-c` for context size):

```bash
llama-server \
```

title: Eval bug: ggml-hexagon on Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 (SM7750, HTP v73) - HMX MUL_MAT returns inf for n>=5, FLASH_ATTN_EXT and GATED_DELTA_NET fail, garbled output
body:
### Name and Version

```
$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=./lib ADSP_LIBRARY_PATH=./lib ./bin/llama-cli --version
ggml-hex: forcing ndev to 1 for SoCs archs lower than v75.
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 1, commit 86a24a1)
built with Clang 21.0.0 for Android aarch64
```

Built with the official toolchain image `ghcr.io/snapdragon-toolchain/arm64-android:v0.7`, preset `arm64-android-snapdragon-release` from `docs/backend/snapdragon/CMakeUserPresets.json`, installed to `/data/local/tmp/llama.cpp` and run from `adb shell` as described in `docs/backend/snapdragon/README.md`.

### Operating systems

Other? (Please let us know in description)

### GGML backends

Hexagon

### Hardware

Motorola Edge 70 (`roadstr`, XT2601-2), Qualcomm **Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 (SM7750)**, Hexagon **v73**, 12 GB LPDDR5X.

```
ggml-hex: Loading driver libcdsprpc.so
ggml-hex: forcing ndev to 1 for SoCs archs lower than v75.
ggml-hex: FASTRPC_GET_DOMAINS query failed (0x6c), using static CDSP domains
ggml-hex: Hexagon backend (experimental) : allocating new registry : ndev 1
ggml-hex: Hexagon Arch version v73, DMA64 disabled
ggml-hex: device 0: HTP0 (phys=0, virt=0, domain=cdsp:3)
```

OS: Android 16. Full disclosure: the phone runs an unofficial LineageOS 23.2 build, but vendor, DSP and firmware images are stock Motorola (`ro.vendor.build.fingerprint = motorola/roadstr_g/roadstr:16/W1WRS36.39-115-2/549c34:user/release-keys`). `ro.soc.model = SM7750`.

### Models

- `bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF` — `Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf`
- `unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF` — `Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_0.gguf`

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On SM7750 / v73 the Hexagon backend runs fast but produces garbled output for both models. The CPU backend on the same device, same binaries and same prompt answers correctly.

**Reproduce (greedy, same prompt):**

```
./bin/llama-completion -m models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf -t 4 -n 50 --temp 0 -no-cnv -p "$PROMPT" -dev none -ngl 0
  -> "I'm not aware of any Snapdragon phone chip that has three processors that can run a neural network. ..."

./bin/llama-completion -m models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf -t 4 -n 50 --temp 0 -no-cnv -p "$PROMPT" -dev HTP0 -ngl 99
  -> "lius (1872)). The Americans are indifferent to the best. However, don't have a brother (sister), 1968, Virginia, ..."
```

Qwen3.5-4B behaves the same way: correct on CPU, mixed-script garbage on `HTP0`.

**`test-backend-ops -b HTP0` narrows it down to three ops:**

1. **MUL_MAT through HMX fails for n >= 5** (n = 1 passes). With `GGML_HEXAGON_MM_SELECT=1` (HVX only) MUL_MAT passes: 761 OK, 0 FAIL. `GGML_HEXAGON_NHMX=1`, `GGML_HEXAGON_HOSTBUF=0` and `GGML_HEXAGON_VMEM=0` do not help (89 FAIL each).
   ```
   [MUL_MAT] ERR = inf > 0.000500000   MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0,type_b=f32,m=16,n=5,k=256,bs=[1,1],nr=[1,1],per=[0,1,2,3],k_v=0,o=1,src_overlap=0): FAIL
   [MUL_MAT] ERR = inf > 0.000500000   MUL_MAT(type_a=q8_0,type_b=f32,m=6,n=4096,k=5120,bs=[1,1],nr=[1,1],per=[0,1,2,3],k_v=0,o=1,src_overlap=0): FAIL
   ```
2. **FLASH_ATTN_EXT** (1869 failing cases in the full run with `MM_SELECT=1`):
   ```
   [FLASH_ATTN_EXT] ERR = inf > 0.000500000   FLASH_ATTN_EXT(hsk=64,hsv=64,nh=8,nr23=[4,1],kv=1024,nb=32,mask=1,sinks=0,max_bias=0.000000,logit_softcap=0.000000,prec=f32,type_K=f16,type_V=f16,permute=[0,1,2,3],kv_view=1,v_is_view_of_k=0,n_kv_max=0): FAIL
   ```
3. **GATED_DELTA_NET**:
   ```
   [GATED_DELTA_NET] ERR = 10275358628165832.000000000 > 0.000000100   GATED_DELTA_NET(type=f32,head_count=4,head_size=64,n_seq_tokens=64,n_seqs=1,v_repeat=1,permuted=0,kda=0,K=1): FAIL
   [GATED_DELTA_NET] ERR = inf > 0.000000100   GATED_DELTA_NET(type=f32,head_count=4,head_size=64,n_seq_tokens=256,n_seqs=1,v_repeat=1,permuted=0,kda=0,K=1): FAIL
   ```

ADD / SUB / DIV also show a few f16 failures, but these are tiny precision deltas (ERR ~1.5e-7 vs 1e-7 threshold) and look harmless; MUL passes 67/67.

**Workaround that gives correct output:** `GGML_HEXAGON_MM_SELECT=1 GGML_HEXAGON_OPFILTER='^(FLASH_ATTN_EXT|GATED_DELTA_NET)$'` plus `-fa off`. Output then matches the CPU backend for both models, but without HMX the NPU is slower than the CPU, so the backend currently brings no benefit on this SoC:

| Llama-3.2-1B Q4_0, `-t 4` | pp512 t/s | tg64 t/s | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 216.3 | 34.4 | correct |
| HTP0, default (HMX) | 1749.4 | 29.9 | garbled |
| HTP0, workaround above | 78.7 | 27.0 | correct |

| Qwen3.5-4B Q4_0, `-t 4` | pp512 t/s | tg64 t/s | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 46.3 | 9.1 | correct |
| GPU (OpenCL, Adreno 722) | 77.5 | 7.5 | correct |
| HTP0, default (HMX) | 437.4 | 8.1 | garbled |
| HTP0, workaround above | 25.6 | 6.2 | correct |

My guess, not verified: the HMX / FA / GDN kernels assume something about v73 that holds on Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 but not on the 7-series part (VTCM size or HMX configuration?). Similar reports for other SoCs were #25876 (SM8850, v81) and #24365 (SM8845, v81).

I have the toolchain set up and can rebuild and test patches or run extra diagnostics on this device.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown — first build of the Hexagon backend on this device was at `86a24a1`.

### Relevant log output

```
$ GGML_HEXAGON_MM_SELECT=1 ./bin/test-backend-ops -b HTP0   (failures grouped by op)
   1869 FLASH_ATTN_EXT
     33 DIV        (f16, ERR ~1e-7)
     14 ADD        (f16, ERR ~1e-7)
     12 MUL        (full run only; `-o MUL` alone passes 67/67)
      7 GATED_DELTA_NET
      1 SUB        (f16, ERR ~1e-7)
```

title: Eval bug: test-save-load-state aborts on hrm_text with GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC (input-layer tensor makes the backend assignment depend on batch size)
body:
### Name and Version

version: b11194-5-g86a24a182 (master 86a24a182)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA, HIP, Vulkan

### Hardware

RTX 4070 (local).
ggml-ci: T4, ROCm, Intel PTL, Apple.

### Models

`hrm_text-dense.gguf` from `test-generate-models` (any `LLM_ARCH_HRM_TEXT` model).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Test 9 added by #27530 exposes an existing HRM-Text issue under `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC`: `test-save-load-state` aborts on `hrm_text-dense.gguf` in several GPU ctest jobs of ggml-ci (CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan on Intel Linux / NVIDIA / Apple) with `unexpected graph reallocation` (for example: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/actions/runs/36226612703/job/108361769531#step:3:1272). The CPU job passes.

The failure is not in the restore path itself. Test 9 first decodes 8 tokens to obtain the baseline, clears memory, and then decodes 24 tokens. The abort occurs during this second `llama_decode()` (`tests/test-save-load-state.cpp:721`), before any corrupted state is restored.

Cause: `hrm.z_l_init` is registered as `LLM_TENSOR_LAYER_INPUT` (`src/llama-arch.cpp`), so it lives in host memory. The `ggml_add()` with the embeddings in `src/models/hrm-text.cpp` therefore goes through the scheduler's offload rule and is assigned to the GPU only for batches >= 32 rows. The reserve graph (100 tokens) puts it on the GPU, small decodes put it on the CPU, so the allocator is re-reserved for the 8-token graph and the 24-token decode needs another reallocation (`ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc: node embd is not valid`), which `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC` turns into the abort. Without that option it only costs an extra reallocation.

`LLM_TENSOR_TOKEN_EMBD_NORM` avoids the same problem by being placed on the first layer instead of the input layer; doing the same for `hrm.z_l_init` (`LLM_TENSOR_LAYER_REPEATING`, bid 0) makes `test-save-load-state --models` pass 127/127 on CUDA and CPU with `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC=ON`.

Repro: build with `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC=ON`, then `test-save-load-state -m tests/test-models/hrm_text-dense.gguf`.

### First Bad Commit

08618ff8e (#27530) exposes it by adding test 9; the placement dates from 7d6f5d02b (#27625).

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```
hrm_text-dense.gguf      ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:1622: ggml_backend_sched_alloc_splits: unexpected graph reallocation (graph size = 385, nodes = 385, leafs = 80), debug_realloc = 1
#10 test_state_restore_failure (...) at tests/test-save-load-state.cpp:721
```
</details>

title: Qwen3.5-4B: first request after load is extremely slow (CUDA backend), warm performance is fine (RTX 2060 / sm_75, b11206)
body:
llama.cpp b11206 (2b129ccfa), Windows x64 release binaries (cuda-12.4 and vulkan).

- GPU: RTX 2060 6 GB (sm_75), driver 610.88; CPU i7-9750H; Windows 11 Pro
- Model: unsloth Qwen3.5-4B, Q4_K_M GGUF

Qwen3.5-4B (hybrid Gated DeltaNet): the first chat completion after model load is extremely slow; requests from the third on run at normal speed. Startup warmup at defaults; `/health` reports ok before the slow first request.

```
llama-server.exe -m Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 16384 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --reasoning-budget 0 --no-webui
```

|---|---|---|---|
| CUDA | 1st | 0.44 tok/s | 3.09 tok/s |

| Vulkan | 1st | 6.4 tok/s | 15.4 tok/s |
| Vulkan | 3rd+ | 84-90 tok/s | 47.0 tok/s |

Is the first-request cost expected for the GDN layers (per-slot state or graph init), and is issuing one warm-up request per slot the right mitigation? I can test PR builds on this card.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I'm running llama.cpp in router model. I configured 2 machines to use RPC long ago to run larger models but I found it useful to run 3 models in parallel when working with certain software like Hermes agent and OpenWebUI.

**Main**: Qwen 3.6 27B Q8 - running with **tensor** **split** on dual R9700

When running both Main and Aux in this "mixed mode" it starts working but after a while I get a slow down followed by an error with main model being offloaded or occasionally a full crash. It doesn't seem to be a VRAM issue or system resources.

Any thoughts on whether this is feasible or if there's a way to get **Gemma 4 12B** running with **tensor split** and ROCM. I'd like to use Vulkan but that doesn't work at with tensor split. I could switch the delegate model to another machine but then I'd need to run something smaller.

title: Misc. bug: Hexagon ADD reads wrong rows when dim 1 broadcasts across dim 2 slices
body:
### Name and Version

Current upstream `master` at `f805c57a2d0b7cc171e599303ce2040f6e1bfe15` (the same path is present in `6e0962b6f60b73ec9e6c0d428d4503151a8ee3d3`).

### Backend

Hexagon HTP, `GGML_OP_ADD` with F32 or F16 operands.

### Problem description and steps to reproduce

Use `src0` with GGML dimensions `[N, R, B, 1]` and `src1` with dimensions `[N, 1, B, 1]`, where `N > 1`, `R > 1`, and `B > 1`. For example, `[128, 4, 8, 1]` plus `[128, 1, 8, 1]`. Fill each dim-2 slice of `src1` with a distinct finite value and compare `ggml_add(src0, src1)` on HTP with CPU. Every row in a dim-2 slice should use the same `src1` row. The reported symptom is `FLT_MAX` / `inf` output.

Static code-path analysis shows a mismatch:

1. [Host dispatch](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f805c57a2d0b7cc171e599303ce2040f6e1bfe15/ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/ggml-hexagon.cpp#L5001-L5006) classifies this as `HTP_BINARY_KERNEL_SAME_SHAPE`: `ne11 == 1` satisfies `is_same_shape`, but `ne12 > 1` excludes `HTP_BINARY_KERNEL_ROW_BCAST`.
2. [The same-shape HTP worker](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f805c57a2d0b7cc171e599303ce2040f6e1bfe15/ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/binary-ops.c#L502-L516) starts at `i11 = 0` but copies `current_block_size` `src1` rows with source stride `nb11`. When a block contains at least two rows, the second copy reads the next dim-2 slice instead of repeating the current row. The last slice can read past `src1`.

The existing [binary broadcast test cases](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f805c57a2d0b7cc171e599303ce2040f6e1bfe15/tests/test-backend-ops.cpp#L9700-L9730) do not appear to include this exact shape pattern.

This report is based on source analysis and the reported output symptom; I do not have an on-device log to attach.

Description:
The llama.cpp OpenAI-compatible server currently supports endpoints like /v1/chat/completions, but does not support the newer OpenAI Responses API (/v1/responses).

Many OpenAI client SDKs and tools are moving toward the unified Responses API, which supports structured outputs, tool calls, and multimodal responses in a single endpoint. Lack of /v1/responses support makes it harder to use llama.cpp as a drop-in replacement for OpenAI backends without an additional proxy or translation layer.

Requested feature:
Add native support for the /v1/responses endpoint in llama-server, aligned as closely as possible with OpenAI’s Responses API request/response format.

Benefits:

Improved compatibility with modern OpenAI SDKs

Easier migration from OpenAI APIs to llama.cpp

Reduced need for custom proxy or request rewriting layers

Thanks for the great work on llama.cpp!

### Motivation

I want to use ClaudeCode with llama-server offline, but it currently don't support necessary endpoints.

title: Offloaded-MoE prefill leaves the GPU idle waiting on serial expert H2D copies (single-GPU -ncmoe)
body: Sharing a performance finding from profiling the offloaded-MoE path (`--n-cpu-moe` / `-ncmoe`) — the setup where a big MoE model runs on a small GPU with the experts kept in system RAM and streamed in per layer. My box: RTX 3060 12GB, Ryzen 5600X, 32GB DDR4, PCIe 4.0, Ubuntu 24.04. Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Q4_K_M), `-ncmoe 26`, prefill at pp2048 / ub2048. Everything below is single-box and gen4-specific, so numbers will move on other hardware. On this setup prefill is bottlenecked by PCIe transfers, not GPU compute. Profiling with Nsight, the GPU sits idle a large fraction of each prefill pass waiting on expert-weight H2D copies, and those copies run serially with the matmul that consumes them — layer N's weights finish uploading, then layer N computes, then N+1's weights start uploading. The upload and the compute don't overlap on the offload path. Two changes helped a lot, both prefill-only and both producing token-identical output at temp 0: 1. Page-locking the mmap-backed CPU expert weights so the H2D transfers DMA directly instead of going through a pageable bounce buffer. ~+21% on its own. 2. Overlapping the expert uploads with compute on a second stream with a few staging slots, so layer N+1's weights upload while layer N is still computing. This is where most of the win is. Together that took prefill from ~1143 to ~1880 tok/s at identical settings — roughly +64%, pure code, no config change. GPU idle during prefill dropped from ~42% to a few percent. I prototyped both behind env flags on a fork so I could A/B them on the same binary and confirm the output stayed identical: https://github.com/thecodacus/llama.cpp/tree/fable5/prefetch-experts (there's a benchmark writeup in the branch with the exact commands and the full before/after log). I'm raising this as a finding rather than a PR — partly because AGENTS.md asks for that, and partly because the right way to expose something like this upstream is probably whoever owns the CUDA scheduler deciding on the shape, not me dropping a patch on you. Two honest caveats: this was measured a few weeks back at around the b6xxx era, and the CUDA backend has moved since, so the exact idle percentage may be stale — I haven't re-run against current master. And I know pipeline copies are already a thing for the multi-device case; the gap I'm describing is specifically the single-GPU offload path, which always gets `n_copies = 1`. Main question for maintainers: is reducing GPU idle on the offload path something you'd want addressed, and if so, is overlap-on-a-second-stream the right approach — or is there a reason the offload copies are serial today that I'm not seeing? Happy to share nsys timelines or run other configs if that's useful. here is nsys trace

title: Feature request: run MoE expert weights from host RAM via PCIe DMA (no H2D copy) — 23GB MoE on 1.6GB VRAM, 81GB Qwen3-235B on 8GB cards
body:
## TL;DR

For MoE models, keep expert weights in host memory (pinned buffer) and let cuBLAS read them **directly over PCIe DMA** — never copy experts into VRAM. Non-expert layers stay in VRAM as usual. Result (RTX 4090, real measurements):

| Model | Standard (all-in-VRAM) | This approach | VRAM saved | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite Q2_K (23.3GB) | 23.3GB VRAM, 65 t/s | **1.6GB VRAM, 37.5 t/s** | −93% | 58% retained |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (11GB) | OOM on 8GB cards | **2.1GB VRAM, 46.8 t/s** | — | ≈ parity |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B Q2_K (81.7GB) | impossible on consumer GPUs | **8GB VRAM (verification in progress)** | — | TBD |

## Motivation

The biggest real-world MoE use case is running a large model on a small GPU. With all experts in VRAM, an 8GB card tops out around a 7-8B dense or a ~11GB MoE. But MoE experts are only *activated* sparsely (2-8 of 256 per token) — the full weight set doesn't need to live on the GPU. The bottleneck is that llama.cpp's offload path copies expert weights H2D per layer (see #25859), and the `--n-cpu-moe` path computes experts on CPU (slow).

## Proposed approach (high level)

1. Load expert weights into a **host pinned buffer** (not GPU VRAM, not anonymous mmap that gets evicted).
2. Run the expert matmuls on GPU via **cuBLAS operating directly on host pointers** — the CUDA driver DMA-reads the expert weights from host RAM over PCIe on demand, per activated expert. No H2D staging copy, no per-layer streaming.
3. VRAM holds only non-expert layers + KV cache. For DS-V2-Lite that's ~1.6GB total.
4. Optional: a small expert cache (a few slots, LRU) that D2D-copies the *hot* experts into VRAM once and reuses them — helps when the same experts fire repeatedly (e.g. long prompts / codegen patterns).

## Measured results (RTX 4090, 2026-08-02)

- **DeepSeek-V2-Lite Q2_K**: VRAM 23.3GB → **1.6GB**; speed 37.5 t/s (vs 65 t/s fully offloaded — reasonable PCIe price for −93% VRAM). Expert cache at 0.25: prompt throughput 99 → **308 t/s (+211%)**, gen +5%.
- **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B**: VRAM **2.1GB**, 46.8 t/s — an 11GB MoE that OOMs an 8GB card normally, now runs on ~2GB with near-full speed.
- **Qwen3-235B-A22B Q2_K (81.7GB)**: download in progress; target: run on 8GB VRAM (experts ~80GB in host RAM + PCIe DMA).

## Why this is different from existing work

- #26414 (pin hot experts in RAM via mlock): keeps experts in *system RAM* but still computes them on CPU (or pages them back) — this keeps expert compute on **GPU** with DMA reads.
- #25859 (-ncmoe H2D copies serial): that path still copies weights into VRAM per layer; this approach reads them **in place from host memory** — the copy disappears entirely.
- #23855 (spill-over / MoE GPUs): multi-GPU layout question; orthogonal.

This also composes with existing features: `--n-cpu-moe`-style flag to select the expert storage mode, GGML_OP_OFFLOAD_MIN_BATCH to control when offload kicks in, and the expert cache as an optional accelerator.

## Ask

- Would the maintainers accept a **host-pinned expert buffer + DMA-direct expert matmul** path as an official load mode (e.g. `--expert-mode host-dma`)?
- Happy to open a PR with the CUDA backend changes (it's a focused patch: model loader + CUDA expert matmul path + optional small expert cache).
- Open to discussion on trade-offs: PCIe bandwidth vs VRAM, multi-GPU, pageable vs pinned, and whether a `--host-ram-budget` knob makes sense.

## Context

- All numbers above are from a single RTX 4090 box, measured with llama.cpp-based server (this is a custom fork, patch described at high level above).
- Env: Linux x86_64, CUDA 12, PCIe 4.0 (gen4 single-GPU).
- Happy to provide full benchmark methodology / logs on request.

title: [RPC] SET_ROWS can write past an output tensor buffer in release builds
body:
### Name and Version

`ggml-rpc-server` at commit `15586e2d7165` (tag `b10298`), tested on Linux with ASan and plain RelWithDebInfo builds.

### Affected Module

The ggml RPC backend (`ggml/src/ggml-rpc`) and the CPU `SET_ROWS` kernel.

### Problem description

I found the write-side counterpart to the GET_ROWS out-of-bounds read reported in #26825. An RPC client can send a GRAPH_COMPUTE request with mismatched SET_ROWS tensor shapes, causing the worker to write attacker-controlled data past the output buffer.

ggml_set_rows() requires dst.ne[2] == src0.ne[2] and dst.ne[3] == src0.ne[3], but RPC graph reconstruction bypasses these checks. The CPU kernel only checks them with plain assert(), which is removed when NDEBUG is enabled.

The output offset is also controllable. ggml_nbytes() does not include a dimension's stride when its size is 1, so setting dst.ne[2] = 1 leaves dst.nb[2] out of the RPC buffer-size check. With src0.ne[2] = 2, the kernel reaches i02 = 1 and writes at dst.data + dst.nb[2]. This gives the client a controlled overwrite at a chosen offset relative to dst; it is not an arbitrary write to any process address.

### Reproduce

[rpc_setrows_oob_write.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30942564/rpc_setrows_oob_write.py)

```bash
cd ~/llama.cpp # use the b10298 (15586e2d7) checkout
cmake -B build-rpc-asan -DGGML_RPC=ON -DGGML_SANITIZE_ADDRESS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer" \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer" \
  -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address"
cmake --build build-rpc-asan --target ggml-rpc-server -j"$(nproc)"
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 \
  ./build-rpc-asan/bin/ggml-rpc-server -H 127.0.0.1 -p 50053
```
```bash
python3 rpc_setrows_oob_write.py 50053
```

The default case uses a 16-byte `dst` buffer and places the write immediately after it.

The RPC server should reject a SET_ROWS graph with incompatible tensor shapes before running the kernel.

Replacing assert(ne2 == ne02) and assert(ne3 == ne03) with GGML_ASSERT prevented the write in both builds. A valid SET_ROWS request still produced the expected output. Rejecting the malformed graph at the RPC layer would be preferable to aborting the process.

This uses the same RPC graph-reconstruction path as #26825. I am reporting it as a regular issue because `SECURITY.md` says the RPC backend should not be exposed to an untrusted network and the private disclosure program is currently disabled.

title: Profile prefil(tokenizer firstly)
Performance regressions on Android arm64 CPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2): text generation ~8% slower since b10333, prompt processing ~13% slower since b10369
body:
### Summary

Two separate CPU performance regressions on Android arm64 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2), measured with the official `llama-bXXXXX-bin-android-arm64.tar.gz` release binaries, CPU backend only:

1. **Text generation is ~8 % slower in b10333 than in b10092**, and slightly worse again by b10369.
2. **Prompt processing regressed a further ~13 % between b10333 and b10369** (it was at parity between b10092 and b10333).

| Median | b10092 | b10333 | b10369 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Decode tok/s (192-token generations) | **15.48** | 14.26 (0.921×) | 13.92 (0.899×) |
| Prompt tok/s (~2k-token prompt) | 72.7 | **73.9** (1.017×) | 64.5 (0.887×) |

### Environment

- Device: Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra (SM-S918B), Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, Android 16 / API 36
- Binaries: unmodified official release archives, e.g. `llama-b10369-bin-android-arm64.tar.gz`; the runtime auto-selects the armv9.2 CPU variant
- Model: Qwen3.5-2B `Q4_K_M` (bartowski conversion), 1.30 GiB, fully resident, no swap activity

### Method

`llama-server` run under the shell UID with:

```
llama-server -m Qwen_Qwen3.5-2B-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18080 \
  -c 10240 -np 1 -t 5 -tb 8 -Cr 3-7 --cpu-strict 1 -Crb 0-7 --cpu-strict-batch 1 \
  --jinja --no-webui
```

Non-streaming `/v1/chat/completions` requests with `temperature 0`; decode and prompt rates read back from the response `timings` object, so the numbers are the server's own.

Thermal control, since this class of device throttles enough to reorder any comparison:

- every series starts only after battery temperature ≤ 30.0 °C and with charging disabled;
- big-core `scaling_max_freq / cpuinfo_max_freq` headroom is recorded next to every sample;
- the first (page-cache warm-up) sample of every series is discarded;
- decode = 7 samples × 192 tokens; prompt = 4 samples of a ~2,000-token prompt with `cache_prompt: false`.

The regressions are not thermal artifacts: the losing builds ran at **equal or higher** clock headroom than the winning ones (e.g. the b10333 decode series ran entirely at 0.95–1.0 headroom and still lost to a b10092 series that dipped to 0.70).

One observation in the newer builds' favor: server RSS was ~290 MB lower on b10369 (2.66 GB vs 2.95 GB at the same context size).

### What I can offer

- Raw per-sample JSON (rates + thermal headroom per sample) for all six series.
- I can re-run the same harness on candidate builds or bisect the b10092…b10333 window for the decode regression if that helps narrow it down.

title: Feature Request: Add NVFP4 quantization support for KV cache (--cache-type-k / --cache-type-v)
body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Currently, `llama.cpp` supports several quantized formats for KV cache compression (such as `q8_0`, `q4_0`, `f16`, `f8_e5m2`, etc.). While integer 4-bit options like `q4_0` significantly reduce VRAM consumption during long-context inference, floating-point formats generally offer better dynamic range and lower accuracy degradation for attention key/value representations.

With the growing adoption of NVFP4 (NVIDIA FP4) in modern model weights and hardware, having native NVFP4 support for the KV cache would be a huge enhancement for memory-constrained, long-context scenarios.

---

### Describe the solution you'd like

1. Add support for `nvfp4` / `fp4` as valid options for `--cache-type-k` and `--cache-type-v` in `llama-cli`, `llama-server`, and the C++ API.
2. Implement GGML conversion/quantization kernels for NVFP4 KV cache storage and attention computation (leveraging hardware FP4 Tensor Cores where available, with software fallback for unsupported architectures).

---

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **`q4_0` / `q8_0` KV Cache**: While `q8_0` retains near-lossless precision, it takes 8 bits per element. `q4_0` reduces memory to 4 bits but can suffer from accuracy degradation in complex reasoning or coding tasks compared to 4-bit floating-point formats (E2M1 scaling).
- **`fp8` (E4M3 / E5M2)**: Excellent quality, but still requires ~8 bits per element.

---

### Additional context

- **VRAM Savings**: FP4 KV cache cuts KV memory usage by up to 75% compared to FP16, allowing much larger context windows (e.g., 32k–128k+) on consumer GPUs (16GB–24GB VRAM).
- **Target Use Case**: Long-context local agentic workflows (e.g., coding, multi-turn tool calling) where KV cache dominates VRAM footprint.
- **Ecosystem Alignment**: NVFP4 is increasingly becoming a standard FP4 format supported across recent NVIDIA architectures and LLM ecosystems.

### Motivation

As local LLMs (like Qwen3.6-27B and DeepSeek models) rapidly expand their context windows to 32k–128k+, the VRAM consumption of the KV cache frequently exceeds the memory footprint of the model weights themselves. 

While integer 4-bit options (`q4_0`, `q4_1`) are supported in `llama.cpp`, integer quantization often struggles to preserve fine-grained attention weights in long-context reasoning and code generation tasks. FP4 formats (specifically NVFP4 / E2M1 scaling) offer a significantly better dynamic range for attention keys and values at 4-bit precision. 

Adding NVFP4 KV cache support would allow developers running local coding assistants and agentic workflows to handle massive contexts (64k–128k) on consumer GPUs (16GB/24GB VRAM) with minimal accuracy degradation and drastically reduced memory pressure.

### Possible Implementation

1. **GGML Type Definition**:
   - Introduce `GGML_TYPE_NVFP4` (or `GGML_TYPE_FP4`) in `ggml.h` with appropriate block size (e.g., 32 elements per block with FP16/E8M0 scales).

2. **Quantization & CUDA Kernels**:
   - Add FP4 quantization/dequantization routines in `ggml-quants.c` and CUDA backend (`ggml-cuda/`).
   - Implement FP4 unpack/dequantize inline within flash attention / K-V cache lookup kernels (or leverage native FP4 Tensor Core instructions on supported NVIDIA architectures).

3. **CLI & Argument Parsing**:
   - Register `nvfp4` / `fp4` in `common/arg.cpp` for `--cache-type-k` (`-ctk`) and `--cache-type-v` (`-ctv`).

title: Vulkan: qwen3next MoE with IQ1_M router weights produces all-zero/garbage output (works on CPU)
body:
## Environment
- macOS 23.6 (x86_64 Hackintosh), MoltenVK 1.4.2, AMD RX 6750 GRE 12GB
- llama.cpp b10310 (commit 3653e6d), Vulkan backend, self-built with AppleClang 16

## Model
- `nerkyor/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DSV4Pro-SFT-GPT56Sol-RL-Agent-GGUF` Q4 LynnStyle (20.47GB, qwen3next arch, 40 layers, 256 experts top-8, SSM/recurrent layers)
- Tensor type distribution: F32 261 (norms, ssm_a/conv1d/dt), Q8_1 36 (attention), Q4_K 45 + Q5_K 30 + Q6_K 222 + Q8_K 39 (experts/SSM weights), **IQ1_M 40 = all `ffn_gate_inp_shexp.weight` (MoE router)**

## Reproduction
```bash
llama-server -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DSV4Pro-SFT-GPT56Sol-RL-Agent-LynnStyle-Q4-imatrix.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 30 -t 5 -c 8192 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```
Then chat completion with a **multi-line prompt** (e.g. JSON compression instruction with newlines). Output is 300× `0` characters (or garbage tokens), temperature 0.1.

Single-line prompts work fine. Full-CPU (`-ngl 0`) works fine for all prompts.

## Observed
1. Multi-line prompts → all-zero output (`000000...`) or garbage tokens on Vulkan offload
2. After a failed request, **subsequent requests stay corrupted until server restart**
3. Overriding the IQ1_M router + SSM tensors to CPU fixes output quality:
   `--override-tensor "blk\.[0-9]+\.ffn_gate_inp_shexp\.weight=CPU" --override-tensor "blk\.[0-9]+\.ssm_.*=CPU"` → correct output, but ~2 tok/s (too slow)
4. A control model with identical architecture but F32 router weights (`Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf`, qwen35moe arch) works perfectly on Vulkan with same offload settings

## Expected
Correct output on Vulkan backend regardless of prompt formatting

## Analysis
Vulkan backend has full IQ1_M support (dequant_iq1_m.comp, mul_mat_vec_iq1_m.comp, matmul_iq1_m_f16/f32). The failure is structural (all-zero logits → all-zero tokens), not minor precision loss. CPU path produces correct results with the same weights, pointing to a numerical issue in the Vulkan IQ1_M dequant/matmul path (possibly triggered by specific activation patterns from newline tokens in the router input).

## Additional
- Failure state persists across requests until server restart (state pollution)
- Not reproducible on full CPU offload
- Control: UD model (same 35B-A3B MoE + SSM architecture, F32 router) has zero issues on Vulkan

title: mtmd: one-sample audio input causes process abort
body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.2.0-dev (build 10618, commit eb25b7263)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), llama-cli, llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -hf ggml-org/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF --port 18080 -c 4096
# Then send a request to /v1/chat/completions with a single-sample WAV file provided as input_audio.
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When a WAV file containing is exactly one sample, the process aborts at mtmd.cpp:1553 GGML_ASSERT(buf.size() > sizeof(float)). Because one float occupies 4 bytes, the buffer size is also 4 bytes, the condition evaluates to false (4 > 4 is false). 
I verified the crash on Voxtral; the assertion sits on the shared path before the per-model preprocessor is selected, so it should affect all audio models.
The Whisper preprocessor is designed to zero-pad very short audio clips. Therefore, regardless of whether such extremely short input should ultimately be accepted or result in an error, a single request should not trigger an assertion that kills the entire server process. The erroneous assertion causes the entire server process to abort instead of returning an error for the request.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Build any recent master with audio-capable mtmd.
2. Create a 1-sample 16 kHz mono WAV (see attached script).
3. Feed it to llama-mtmd-cli, or POST it to llama-server as input_audio.
4. CLI aborts with exit code 134; the server process dies and /health stops responding.

AI usage disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help troubleshoot this bug and draft this report. I personally reproduced and verified the crash and also understand the relevant code.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. The assertion is long-standing and was not touched by the recent
short-input fix (#26536), which changed min_samples inside the preprocessor but
not this buffer-size guard at the tokenizer entry.

### Relevant log output

title: mtmd: audio with a duration that is a multiple of 30s produces one extra silent chunk
body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.2.0-dev (build 10618, commit eb25b7263)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), llama-cli

### Command line

```shell
llama-mtmd-cli -hf ggml-org/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF --audio 30s.wav -p "T." -n 1 --no-warmup
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When the audio duration is an exact multiple of 30 seconds (or falls within approximately 20ms of the end of a 30-second cycle), the Whisper audio preprocessor generates an extra audio chunk and encodes it separately. This additional chunk consists entirely of trailing padding (silence) and contains no actual audio. In the logs, this manifests as `total = 4` instead of `total = 3` (or `5` instead of `4` for 60-second audio), resulting in an extra encoding operation taking about 550ms.

The Mel spectrogram has approximately 3,001 frames of padding appended to the end. The chunking logic slices the audio every 3,000 frames. When the number of actual audio frames is a multiple of 3,000 (or exactly one less), this padding fills a complete 3,000-frame window; consequently, it is encoded as a normal chunk rather than being discarded. The "skip last incomplete chunk" check in the code (`if (n_len < frames_per_chunk) break;`) only catches incomplete padding chunks; it fails to catch padding chunks that fill a complete window. (Location: `mtmd_audio_preprocessor_whisper::preprocess` in `tools/mtmd/mtmd-audio.cpp`, lines ~597–601.)

The transcription output is unaffected—I compared the output before and after the fix, and it is byte-identical. Therefore, this is a performance and context-usage issue, not a correctness one.The cost is an extra ~187 context tokens (all silence) and ~550ms of encoding time per instance. While the hit rate might appear low (random durations have a ~0.067% chance), slicing long audio into fixed 30-second segments is a common practice in speech processing pipelines, meaning such callers would trigger this issue for every segment.

Based on the code, the `qwen3a` and `gemma4a` preprocessors in the same file already use the "number of valid frames" as the upper bound for the loop and do not suffer from this issue; only the Whisper preprocessor uses the "total length including padding."

I believe the fix is ​​to have the chunking loop terminate when the remaining frames consist entirely of padding (by using the number of valid audio frames as the upper bound). The change is minimal, and I am willing to submit a PR, but I would like to confirm first if the maintainers agree with this approach.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Create a 16 kHz mono WAV whose length is exactly 480000 samples (30.00 s).
2. Run: llama-mtmd-cli -hf ggml-org/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF --audio 30s.wav -p "T." -n 1 --no-warmup
3. The log shows the audio encoded twice (total = 4) instead of once (total = 3).

Observed on my machine (M2 Max, macOS), by audio duration:
| duration     | samples | chunks encoded | expected |
|--------------|---------|----------------|----------|
| 29.98963 s   | 479834  | 1              | 1  OK    |
| 29.99 s      | 479840  | 2              | 1  BUG   |
| 30.00 s      | 480000  | 2              | 1  BUG   |
| 30.01 s      | 480160  | 2              | 2  OK    |
| 60.00 s      | 960000  | 3              | 2  BUG   |
| 90.00 s      | 1440000 | 4              | 3  BUG   |

AI usage disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help troubleshoot this bug and draft this report. I personally reproduced and verified the crash and also understand the relevant code.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Related to #26536 (which fixed a similar duplicate-chunk problem for
short inputs) but on a different boundary: that fix changed min_samples; this case is
the chunk-splitting loop treating a full window of trailing padding as a real chunk.

### Relevant log output

<summary>Logs</summary>


title: server / tokenizer: SIGSEGV (stack overflow) in `unicode_regex_split_stl` — the o200k / GPT4O pre-tokenizer regex recurses once per character, so a ~26,000-character unbroken run of one character class kills the process
body:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 1, commit 4df29be)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Source at `4df29be4f4c3673f428170fda944a5b19f743bb8`, `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`
(`CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE=-O3 -DNDEBUG`), g++ 14.2.0.

The `llama-server` that produced the coredump is a Vulkan build; the `llama-tokenize` used for every
threshold below is a HIP/ROCm build of the same commit with the same flags. The pre-tokenizer path is
CPU-only and identical in both, and both report the same version string.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core), llama-server, llama-tokenize

### Command line

```shell
llama-server \
  --model gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf \
  --n-gpu-layers 99 --ctx-size 131072 --parallel 2 --cont-batching \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 --load-mode none \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 --metrics --no-ui --no-slots
```

None of these flags is load-bearing. The crash is in pre-tokenization, before anything
backend-, batch- or KV-related is reached, and `llama-tokenize` reproduces it with no GPU at all.

### Problem description

**A single POST to `/v1/chat/completions` whose prompt contains a long unbroken run of one character
class terminates the server process with SIGSEGV, during tokenization, before any inference
happens.** It takes ~26,000 characters at the default 8 MiB stack. There is no error, no 4xx and no
log line — the process is simply gone, taking every slot's KV cache and prompt cache with it.

It requires no `tools`, no grammar, no streaming and no concurrency.

**What matters is the longest unbroken run that one alternative of the pre-tokenizer expression can
consume, not the prompt length.** libstdc++'s executor recurses once per repetition, and *every*
quantified alternative in this expression is a driver — not only the letter ones. Measured against
the shipped `llama-tokenize` at an 8 MiB stack, exit 139 = SIGSEGV:

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `'x' * 26,000` → ok · `'x' * 26,500` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'X' * 26,000` → ok · `'X' * 26,250` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'日' * 26,000` → ok · `'日' * 26,250` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'.' * 26,000` → ok · `'.' * 27,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `' ' * 26,000` → ok · `' ' * 28,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'_' * 36,000`, `'\n' * 36,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| English letters, spaces removed — 35,000 | **SIGSEGV** |
| Japanese, punctuation removed — 30,000 | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'Xx' * 18,000` — 36,000 alternating-case letters | ok |
| `'1234567890' * 6,600` — 66,000 digits | ok |
| English prose *with* spaces — 66,000 | ok |
| Japanese *with* ordinary `。` and `、` — 51,000 | ok |

Reading the alternation, three kinds of run recurse:

- **letters of a single case** — `((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+` drives lowercase runs and
  `((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))+` drives uppercase runs. A case change breaks both, which is why
  `'Xx' * 18,000` survives while `'x' * 26,500` and `'X' * 26,250` each die. Non-ASCII letters sit in
  **both** classes.
- **non-letter, non-digit, non-space characters** — ` ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n/]*`, so a long run of a
  single punctuation or symbol character is its own driver.
- **whitespace** — `\s*[\r\n]+`, `\s+(?!\S)`, `\s+`.

**Digits are the exception**: `\p{N}{1,3}` is bounded, so 66,000 digits tokenize fine.

So a space or a full stop ends a *letter* run but opens a run of its own. What keeps ordinary text
safe is that it alternates *short* runs of different classes — prose interleaves letter runs of a
dozen characters with one-character space runs, and neither approaches the threshold. Measured:
66,000 characters of English prose and 51,000 codepoints of Japanese with `。` and `、` both
tokenize normally.

**Non-ASCII does not lower the codepoint threshold.** `unicode_regex_split` collapses each non-ASCII
codepoint to a single category byte, so one CJK codepoint costs the same stack as one ASCII letter —
`'日'` brackets at 26,000 / 26,250, identical to `'X'`. What differs for scripts without inter-word
spaces is that long unbroken letter runs arise there naturally, where in English they have to be
constructed.

**It is reachable by an untrusted caller without anything exotic**: a ~26 KB body of one repeated
character — a letter, a space, a full stop — kills the process, repeatedly. `set_payload_max_length`
is never called anywhere in the tree outside its own definition in the vendored cpp-httplib, so
there is no size cap in front of it, and tokenization happens *before* the context-length check
(`tokenize_input_prompts` at `tools/server/server-context.cpp:4198`, inside
`handle_completions_impl`; the "exceeds the available context size" check is at `:3115`, after the
task is queued), so `--ctx-size` does not bound it either.

We have not surveyed which real-world content reaches ~26,000 characters of one class. The cases we
can name are programmatically whitespace-stripped text, a pathologically long single-case identifier
or concatenated token stream, and long runs of padding, separator or indentation characters.

### Root cause

`gpt-oss` resolves to `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` (o200k_harmony, `case` label at
`src/llama-vocab.cpp:428`). Its pre-tokenizer expression is `src/llama-vocab.cpp:433`:

```
[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))*((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|…)?|
[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))+((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))*(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|…)?|
\p{N}{1,3}| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n/]*|\s*[\r\n]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+
```

That string is **not** in `unicode_regex_split_custom()`'s list of hand-written fast paths
(`src/unicode.cpp:1050`), so every tokenize call for this vocab falls through to
`unicode_regex_split_stl()` (`src/unicode.cpp:739`, reached from `:1367`) and therefore to
libstdc++'s `std::regex`, whose executor is a **recursive** backtracking DFS.

The worst driver is:

```
((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+
```

a lookahead **inside** a greedy repetition. libstdc++ recurses once per repetition
(`_M_dfs` → `_M_rep_once_more` → `_M_dfs`, with `_M_lookahead` allocating on each step), so **stack
depth is proportional to the length of the run being consumed**. After the `\p{...}` →
collapsed-class substitution the lookahead class is `[\xD2A-Za-z]`; `\xD2` is the marker every
non-ASCII letter collapses to (`k_ucat_cpt`, `src/unicode.cpp:1231`), which is why a CJK codepoint
costs exactly the same stack as an ASCII letter.

The lookahead is not required for the recursion — it only makes each frame bigger. The plain
repetitions ` ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+` and `\s+` recurse as well, which is what the `'.'` and `' '` rows
above are showing.

Depth measured from a real core: the faulting thread was **78,124 frames** deep on an 8 MiB stack,
i.e. **~107 bytes per frame**. Combining that with the threshold table below (3,250 characters per
MiB, so ~323 bytes of stack per input character) gives ~3 frames per input character. The core came
from a request containing a 36,000-character run, but the stack was exhausted ~26,000 characters
into it — the process never reached the end of the run.

### Backtrace

Faulting thread is an `httplib::ThreadPool` worker, in request intake. Outermost frames, from `gdb`
on the core (`coredumpctl` only stores 64 frames, all of which are interior to the regex executor —
the caller is invisible without unwinding the whole stack):

```
#0     ?? (libc.so.6+0xa14ba)
#1     malloc
#2     operator new(unsigned long)
#3     std::__detail::_Executor<…>::_M_lookahead(long)
#4     std::__detail::_Executor<…>::_M_dfs(_Match_mode, long)
#5     std::__detail::_Executor<…>::_M_rep_once_more(_Match_mode, long)
…      _M_dfs / _M_rep_once_more, 78,099 frames
#78102 std::__detail::__regex_algo_impl<…>
#78103 unicode_regex_split_stl<char>(…)                       libllama.so
#78104 unicode_regex_split(…)                                 libllama.so
#78105 llm_tokenizer_bpe_session::tokenize(…)                  libllama.so
#78106 llama_vocab::impl::tokenize(…)                          libllama.so
#78107 llama_vocab::tokenize(…)                                libllama.so
#78109 common_tokenize(…)                                     libllama-common.so
#78110 tokenize_mixed(…)                                      libllama-server-impl.so
#78111 tokenize_input_subprompt(…)                            libllama-server-impl.so
#78112 tokenize_input_prompts(…)                              libllama-server-impl.so
#78113 server_routes::handle_completions_impl(…)              libllama-server-impl.so
#78114 std::_Function_handler<unique_ptr<server_http_res>…>   (two handler frames)
#78116 server_http_context::post(…)                          libllama-server-impl.so
#78117 httplib::Server::dispatch_request(…)
#78118 httplib::Server::process_request(…)
#78119 httplib::Server::process_and_close_socket(int)
#78120 httplib::ThreadPool::worker(bool)
#78121 (libstdc++) → #78122 (libc) → #78123 clone
```

The same three outermost frames — `tokenize_input_prompts` → `handle_completions_impl` →
`httplib::ThreadPool::worker` — appear on **4 of 4** coredumps examined. Only the one dump above was
unwound in full.

Note that the crash is on a **spawned** thread, whose stack size is fixed at creation. It is not the
main thread and it cannot grow. `httplib`'s `ThreadPool` does not set a stack size, so on glibc these
workers get `RLIMIT_STACK`'s soft value; the only `pthread_attr_setstacksize` call anywhere in the
tree is in vendored `miniaudio`, which is not on this path.

### Steps to Reproduce

All of the below were run against `gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf`, whose `tokenizer.ggml.pre` is `gpt-4o`.
Any GGUF whose `tokenizer_pre` is `gpt-4o`, `llama4`, `kanana2` or `talkie` selects the same
expression (`src/llama-vocab.cpp:2307`), as does `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_MINIMAX_M2`, which shares the
`case`. `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GRANITE_EMB_MULTI` (`granite-embed-multi-97m`,
`src/llama-vocab.cpp:442`) has the same two lookahead-inside-greedy-repetition drivers with `\p{M}`
added, and is likewise absent from `unicode_regex_split_custom()`, so it should be affected
identically — its own source comment notes the expression family is chosen to *"avoid excessive
backtracking"*, which is the hazard rather than the safeguard here. **We only tested the one GGUF**, so
treat the rest as inference from the source.

**1 · `llama-tokenize` — one command, no GPU, no inference** (loads `vocab_only`, ~0.8 s; it still
needs the GGUF present):

```shell
python3 -c "open('/tmp/x.txt','w').write('x'*36000)"
llama-tokenize -m gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf -f /tmp/x.txt --ids
# → Segmentation fault (core dumped)

python3 -c "open('/tmp/x.txt','w').write('x'*20000)"
llama-tokenize -m gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf -f /tmp/x.txt --ids
# → fine
```

Set the limit explicitly if your shell's default differs from 8 MiB — every threshold quoted here is
from `( ulimit -s 8192; llama-tokenize … )`.

**2 · `llama-server` — kills the process:**

```shell
python3 - <<'EOF' > /tmp/body.json
import json
print(json.dumps({"model":"gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf","max_tokens":512,"temperature":0,
                  "stream":False,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"x"*36000}]}))
EOF
curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/chat/completions \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @/tmp/body.json
# → curl: (52) Empty reply from server; the server process is gone with SIGSEGV
```

**3 · The controls that establish what the trigger actually is.** Each line is one
`( ulimit -s 8192; llama-tokenize -m gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf -f FILE --ids )`:

```shell
# DIES — a run of one class, whatever the class is
python3 -c "open('/tmp/a.txt','w').write('x'*36000)"       # lowercase letters
python3 -c "open('/tmp/b.txt','w').write('X'*36000)"       # UPPERCASE letters — also dies
python3 -c "open('/tmp/c.txt','w').write('.'*36000)"       # punctuation — also dies
python3 -c "open('/tmp/d.txt','w').write(' '*36000)"       # spaces — also dies
python3 -c "open('/tmp/e.txt','w').write('日'*36000)"       # CJK letters
python3 -c "open('/tmp/f.txt','w').write('日本語のテキストです'*3000)"   # 30,000 cp, unpunctuated

# SURVIVES — the class changes often enough that no single run gets long
python3 -c "open('/tmp/g.txt','w').write('Xx'*18000)"      # 36,000 letters, alternating case
python3 -c "open('/tmp/h.txt','w').write('1234567890'*6600)"  # 66,000 digits: \p{N}{1,3} is bounded
python3 -c "open('/tmp/i.txt','w').write('吾輩は猫である。名前はまだ無い。どこで生れたか、とんと見当がつかぬ。'*1500)"
```

The `'Xx'` and `'X'` pair is the one worth running first: it shows the run has to be *case-homogeneous*,
and it rules out "long input" as the explanation.

**4 · Self-contained, no llama.cpp and no model** — for confirming the mechanism in isolation. Takes
the same expression, applies the same `\p{...}` → collapsed-class substitution that
`unicode_regex_split()` performs, and iterates with the same `optimize | nosubs` flags. It has an
explicit-`pthread_attr_setstacksize` arm and a default-attribute `std::thread` arm, and bisects both.
**Posted as a follow-up comment on this issue** rather than linked, so nothing here depends on an
external host.

### Measurement: the threshold is linear in stack size

Isolated probe, `-O3 -DNDEBUG`, subject `'x' * N`, bisected to a 500-character bracket:

| thread stack | last N that survived | first N that crashed | chars per MiB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 MiB | 26,000 | 26,500 | 3,250 |
| 16 MiB | 52,000 | 52,500 | 3,250 |
| 32 MiB | 104,500 | 105,000 | 3,265 |
| 64 MiB | 209,500 | 210,000 | 3,273 |
| 128 MiB | 419,000 | 419,500 | 3,273 |

**Cross-checked against the shipped binary:** at the same 8 MiB, `llama-tokenize` survives 26,000
and dies at 26,500 for `'x'`, and at 26,250 for `'X'` and `'日'` — the same bracket as the isolated
probe, so the constant is the real one and not an artefact of the reproducer. The sweep above was
run for `'x'` only; the other classes were bracketed against the shipped binary, not swept.

Raising `RLIMIT_STACK` moves the threshold proportionally (glibc sizes default-attribute thread
stacks from it), which is a usable stopgap for an operator but not a fix: the request body is
unbounded and tokenization runs *before* the context-length check, so a prompt too long to serve
still crashes the process on its way to being rejected.

### Suggested directions

Offered in case they are useful; the maintainers will know which is right for the codebase.

1. **Add o200k / `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` to `unicode_regex_split_custom()`.** It is the same
   treatment GPT-2, LLaMA-3, Qwen2, Qwen3.5, Kimi-K2 and AFMoE already get, and it removes
   `std::regex` from this vocab's path entirely. This is probably the cheapest complete fix, and it
   will also be considerably faster. **#22110 did exactly this for Qwen3.5 after #21919, and #21257 for
   Qwen2 — so this is a path the codebase has already taken twice for the same defect class.**
2. **Bound the subject.** `unicode_regex_split_stl` already iterates over `offsets`; pre-splitting a
   long run on a safe boundary before handing it to `std::regex` would cap depth. Care needed:
   splitting mid-token changes tokenization, so the boundary must be one the expression cannot match
   across.
3. **Refuse rather than crash.** A depth or input-length guard in `unicode_regex_split_stl` that
   throws (the caller already wraps this in a `try` at `src/unicode.cpp:1301` with
   `catch (std::regex_error & e)` at `:1384`) turns a process kill into a 500 for one request. Worth
   having regardless of 1 or 2, because the same recursion exists for every other `std::regex`
   pre-tokenizer path.
4. **Cap the request body** in the server (`set_payload_max_length` is currently never called), so
   an unbounded subject cannot arrive from the network in the first place.

Happy to test any patch against the reproducers above and report back.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected, and probably not a regression — the mechanism is present wherever
`LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` lacks a `unicode_regex_split_custom` fast path, so it likely dates from
o200k support rather than from a change.

**It is, however, a recurrence, and that seems worth saying plainly.** #17636 reported this same
symptom on the same model family — `gpt-oss-120b`, `'A' * 10000`, with real prose of far greater length
unaffected — and it was closed by #17786, which added `optimize | nosubs` to the `std::regex`
construction in `unicode_regex_split_stl`.

**Those flags are present in this build and the crash still occurs.** At `src/unicode.cpp:745`:

```cpp
constexpr auto regex_flags = std::regex_constants::optimize | std::regex_constants::nosubs;
```

They reduce the size of each recursion frame, but the executor still recurses once per repetition, so
depth remains linear in the length of the run and a long enough run still exhausts the stack. That is
why what we measured is a *threshold* rather than a fix: `nosubs` moved the threshold outward, it did
not remove the recursion. The eleven measurements above are all on a tree that contains #17786.

#21919 is the same defect for Qwen3.5, and it was resolved by #22110 — a non-backtracking handler in
`unicode_regex_split_custom()` plus a regression test. That is suggestion 1 below, and it is the
treatment `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` has never received.

### Relevant log output

```
systemd: <unit>.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=11/SEGV
systemd-coredump: Process <pid> (llama-server) of user <uid> dumped core.
```

Nothing is logged by the server itself. The last lines before the fault belong to the *previous*
request completing normally, which is why this initially looks like a crash *after* a successful
generation rather than during intake of the next one.

Windows

llama-server

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next aborts before server readiness when using `--split-mode tensor` on 2x RTX 5090 / CUDA.

The same model and hardware work correctly with `--split-mode layer`.

The failure is:

```text
ggml/src/ggml-backend-meta.cpp:537:
GGML_ASSERT(ret.axis != GGML_BACKEND_SPLIT_AXIS_UNKNOWN) failed
```

I reproduced the tensor-split failure with both KV cache configurations:

```text
layer  1,1 + Q8_0 K / Q8_0 V -> OK
tensor 1,1 + Q8_0 K / Q8_0 V -> ASSERT

tensor 1,1 + Q8_0 K / Q5_1 V -> ASSERT
```

A later `layer` split test with the same `-ts 1,1` ratio also started and served requests successfully, so the `1,1` tensor split ratio itself does not appear to be sufficient to trigger the failure.

There is no DFlash2 drafter, MTP drafter, or speculative decoding involved in this reproduction.

One preserved reproduction used Q8_0 K / Q5_1 V with CUDA graphs disabled:

```shell
GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1 \
./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64-00001-of-00033.gguf \
  -lm mmap \
  -dev CUDA0,CUDA1 \
  -ngl all \
  -sm tensor \
  -ts 1,1 \
  -fit off \
  -ctk q8_0 \
  -ctv q5_1 \
  -c 261888 \
  -np 1 \
  -b 1024 \
  -ub 128 \
  -fa on \
  --jinja
```

The process aborts with exit code 134 before `/health` becomes ready. GPU memory is reclaimed after the abort, and no CUDA OOM is involved in this failure.

I also reproduced the same `SPLIT_AXIS_UNKNOWN` assertion using Q8_0 K / Q8_0 V.

Possibly related to #27829 and #26902.

#27829 reports the same assertion with Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 on ROCm. This reproduction is different because it uses Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on CUDA without DFlash2, MTP, or any speculative drafter.

#26902 reports the same assertion with CUDA tensor split, but with a different model architecture and 4x Tesla T10 GPUs.

This may indicate that the tensor split metadata issue is not specific to DFlash2.

Reproduced on:

```text
llama.cpp 0.3.0-dev
build 10680
commit d7bd3bfca
full commit: d7bd3bfcad3e29c7e49fd26f38c79ee3e9a3fd6b
```
